data.title: Ms. Rachel calls out Ed Sheeran after Macklemore dropped from tour following Palestine support
data.description:
Children’s YouTuber Ms. Rachel criticized reports that Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his ongoing tour because of the rapper’s pro-Palestinian advocacy.

“Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political,” Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote in a Tuesday Instagram post.

On Monday, Macklemore said that stadium owners — among them Robert Kraft of the New England Patriots — urged the British singer to oust him from the Loop Tour due to past comments about Palestine. The rapper has posted several images of himself donning the Palestinian flag and shared several infographics about Israel’s war in Gaza to social media.

Accurso herself has a history of activism. In April 2025, she put out a statement online responding to criticism she faced over her calls for the protection of Palestinian children. The YouTuber star has also spoken out against Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities, having read books to detainees in New Jersey’s Delaney Hall in June.

“All children have the right to food, water, medical care and education. All children should be protected from violence,” she wrote in her 2025 statement.

Per The Hollywood Reporter, pro-Israel groups went after Macklemore earlier this month after he called for a “free Palestine” during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 MetLife Stadium concert. Pop artist Pink criticized the rapper for his pro-Palestinian comments, allegedly pushing for his removal from the tour.

In his own Instagram post Tuesday, Sheeran said that tour promoters, not himself, chose to cut Macklemore from Loop.

“Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me,” the British singer wrote.

“Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he’s silent,” Accurso wrote, referencing Sheeran’s March 2022 performance raising funds for Ukraine after Russia’s invasion.

When his opening act says Palestinians should be free and not in a genocide he lets a billionaire kick him off,” the children’s YouTuber continued.

In an Aug. 2022 Instagram post, Ukrainian band Antytila posed alongside Sheeran with the country’s flag, commending the pop star for “standing by Ukraine.”

“Thank you Ed and all the team! You are great people with huge hearts!” the band wrote.

In a post on Instagram, Macklemore said Sheeran “and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour,” alleging the singer had spoken to him about pro-Palestinian messaging “being hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with.”

The rapper wrote, “I told (Sheeran) if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and when I stood.”

The YouTuber echoed Macklemore in her Tuesday post, saying, “Palestinian kids have been so dehumanized that as they continue to be killed people debate about being political. It’s sick.”

This story was updated at 4:12 p.m. on Sept. 15, 2026.

data.title: Iran war likely to drive up inflation next year, CBO says
data.description:
The U.S. war against Iran is likely to drive up inflation early next year and could cost at least $2 billion a month as long as it continues, according to a new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

The CBO estimated in its Tuesday report that the main economic impact of the conflict is made of pressures caused by the disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea and the reduction of natural gas and oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The reduction in shipments has increased energy prices and because of it, in the first quarter of 2027, inflation is estimated to be 0.5 percentage points higher than what CBO projected in February this year.

“The agency estimates that the higher rates of inflation attributable to the conflict will boost interest rates on Treasury securities. In CBO’s assessment, interest rates on 3-month Treasury bills are nearly 0.2 percentage points higher in 2026 than the agency estimated this past February,” CBO said in the 19-page report. “By the first half of 2027, such rates are less than 0.1 percentage point higher than previously estimated.”

The war against Iran has cost the Pentagon around $38 billion as of Aug. 1 this year, CBO estimated when factoring in replacing expended munitions, flying hours, assets lost in the conflict and increased fuel costs.

The Pentagon told Congress on Aug. 13 that the cost of war has gone up to over $42 billion, The Hill reported on Tuesday.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate during a hearing in July that the estimated cost of the conflict was $37.5 billion.

“Trump’s illegal war with Iran is a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a statement. “This war is a betrayal of the American people, and it needs to end.”

The main cost for the Pentagon would be the “large expenditure” of missile defense interceptors, leaving the U.S. with a reduced inventory for “several years,” according to CBO.

The CBO report came a day after a report from the Pentagon’s watchdog said that U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries – Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes.

The watchdog said that the U.S. conflict with Iran “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” regarding advanced weapons systems.

President Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly said that the U.S. has sufficient weapons stockpiles.

“CBO estimates that the cost to replace the munitions expended through August 1, 2026, is $21.7 billion: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions,” CBO said in the report.

data.title: Senate Democrats press Patel on elections, media: 5 takeaways
data.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel fielded questions on everything from bestiality to whether the FBI might aid in any efforts to interfere in the midterms on Tuesday.

Like his former colleague Attorney General Pam Bondi, he came to the Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing with opposition on Democratic lawmakers, though Patel largely pushed back against Democratic attacks by boasting of arrest records, falling violent crime rates and captured most-wanted felons.

But that did not impress Democrats who see him as benefiting from already ongoing work.

“As far as I’m concerned, the good work being done by the FBI agents and analysts of the sort that you describe as happening in spite of you, not because of you,” Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) said.

Republican lawmakers generally complimented Patel on a job well done, leaving the sparring with the director to the Democrats.

Growing concern over FBI involvement in elections

Numerous Democratic lawmakers posed questions to Patel on whether he would comply with any demands from President Trump to interfere with the coming midterm elections.

Patel initially told Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) he was “aware” of laws prohibiting deployment of armed federal officials to election sites as well as policy barring investigations inside polling places on Election Day.

But exchanges with other lawmakers proved more contentious and resulted in murkier answers.

“Can you commit to this committee that you will not send FBI agents to the polls on Election Day?” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked.

“The FBI will follow the law. If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law. We will, otherwise, we won’t,” Patel said.

Blumenthal said he should have received an “unequivocal, clear, unambiguous commitment that the FBI will be kept out of election interference.”

Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) noted that Trump has claimed that the only way the Democrats could win the midterms is if they cheated.

“The president is completely justified in making his opinions known, as does any president before him,” Patel said, noting the FBI has election crisis coordinators at all 56 field offices.

“It’s the American people, Republicans and Democrats and independents, who have to be the deciders of who their representatives in Congress are, not the President of the United States, not a compliant, servile FBI director who does the will of the president,” Welch said.

Subpoenas to journalists and a claim of perjury 

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) accused Patel of lying about subpoenaing journalists in what turned into a lengthy exchange that prompted Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) to raise his voice and ask the lawmaker if he was “ready to shut up.”

Booker said Patel has given inconsistent statements about the bureau’s practices, noting May testimony in which he said no journalists were being investigated while numerous subpoenas were later issued to reporters.

“Grand jury subpoenas were served on three New York Times reporters; armed FBI agents went to their homes. You subpoenaed their phone company for their call records. You subpoenaed the records of one reporter’s mother. You get upset when somebody writes a fair story about your girlfriend, but you’re out there using the FBI to go after a reporter’s mom,” he said, noting reporters’ spouses’ records were also sought.

Patel maintains the journalists weren’t under investigation but rather information was sought from them as part of an effort to unmask leakers providing information to journalists.

“This administration focuses on the leakers of classified information that endanger the lives of elected officials and American citizens. We are not targeting reporters at any point in time,” he said.

But Booker noted that one of the reporters whose records were subpoenaed wrote a story about Patel’s girlfriend receiving a detail composed of SWAT agents. He pointed to other cases where a judge had admonished the FBI for seeking subpoenas of journalists.

“None of these line up. Somewhere you’re lying. The message that every reporter in America is getting right now is that we have an FBI director that is attacking the most vaunted of our amendments, which is our first one: freedom of the press. If you write about this director, this FBI will run your name through government databases….This man before us using a police agency to settle personal grievances about a story that embarrassed him, and this is not a one-time thing, Mr. Patel,” Booker said.

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) later showed a photo of Patel with a quote from him stating that the media is “the most powerful enemy the United States has ever seen.” 

Travels and tribulations

Patel sought to head off questions about his use of the FBI jet to travel to see his country music singer girlfriend’s concerts or to the 2026 Winter Olympics by releasing a July 20 letter to Grassley ahead of the hearing.

“As Director, I have reimbursed all personal travel and expenses and am fully compliant with and strictly follow the Office of Management and Budget rules,” he wrote in the letter.

Compared with past appearances before Congress, Patel received fewer questions about his travels.

Hirono noted that a VIP snorkel trip at the site of the USS Arizona in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, is “a sacred site. Sacred. That is why these tours are rare.”

“As part of a broader pattern of you using your office to benefit yourself, showing your lack of judgment and character, you have wasted untold taxpayer dollars driving around in foreign luxury cars, partying in Italy, and flying a private jet to play golf and watch hockey. There has been bipartisan criticism. I’m glad to know that some of my Republican colleagues actually criticized some of this activity,” she said.

Patel grew defensive when asked about his trip to Italy for the Winter Olympics by Welch, who noted photos of the director partying with the U.S. men’s national hockey team in their locker room.

“What you’ll never understand is the players who are my friends invited me into the locker room. What you’ll never understand is that during that trip, where 300,000 Americans went to Italy to participate in the Games and watched them, not a single security incident occurred,” he said before going on to reference the extradition of a man held in Italy.

“And the most important thing to come out of that trip, besides the American men defeating the Canadians and celebrating the love of this country and inviting me in to do so is the fact that we obtained the seizure and capture of China’s most prolific hacker and returned him to the United States.”

Frustration over lack of responses

Patel refused to answer several questions posed by Democratic lawmakers, routinely citing ongoing investigations.

He would not answer questions about a Florida-based federal investigation into a number of perceived Trump enemies, including into former CIA Director John Clapper, as well as investigations that included subpoenas of journalists, to various shootings carried out by immigration officers.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), who questioned the director about immigration-related shootings, asked, “why does it take so long” when Patel said he was unable to answer.

“I know some of these shootings and incidents have been more recent, but some go back months and months and months, some to last year,” Padilla said.

Hirono seemed to reference Patel’s posts announcing the arrest of shooters following the assassination of Charlie Kirk and a shooting at Brown University.

“You know you testified today that to questions you don’t feel like answering, ‘it’s ongoing. It’s an investigation. Can’t talk about it.’ And yet you have actually posted things that should be ongoing and where you should keep your mouth shut,” she said.

Questions about bestiality and hiring

In one notable exchange, Patel was asked about a shift in FBI hiring practices that lifted longtime bans on selecting new trainees if they have engaged in prostitution or bestiality.

“When you saw bestiality — I say this with respect to the person who recommended it — why didn’t you just say, ‘What planet did you parachute in from? Why do I want to lead with my chin and get into bestiality?’” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) asked.

Patel acknowledged he had some reservations but said prospective hires could have been trafficked into “degrading acts of all kinds.”

“That was my initial response, senator. But they then explained to me and showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought they should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification. That’s all,” the director said.

Those activities have long been a bar to working at the FBI. Engaging in prostitution is a crime, and the FBI works on sex trafficking cases, while ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) earlier this week said lifting the ban on animal cruelty “are not minor technical adjustments.”

“But you’re not telling us today that if a human being had sex with an animal, that they can still be an FBI agent,” Kennedy asked toward the end of his line of questioning.

“No,” Patel responded.

data.title: Cook Political Report shifts New Hampshire toward Republican Sununu
data.description:
Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, shifted its rating for the New Hampshire Senate race to “toss-up,” a significant move in Republicans’ favor, since Democrats need to keep that seat. 

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) is challenging former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.), who has been out of the Senate for 18 years, for the seat opening up by the retirement of Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. 

A late August poll by the University of New Hampshire showed Sununu and Pappas nearly tied, at 45 percent Sununu to 43 percent Pappas. While other Senate races have shifted in Democrats’ favor in recent months, New Hampshire might be an exception to a national trend. Many New Hampshire voters also favor a Republican for governor, and are generally fond of Sununu, who comes from a popular political family in the state. 

“Even in a light blue state, the amount of money national Republicans have dedicated to this race is a flashing red light for Democrats,” said Jessica Taylor, editor at Cook, in a statement. 

The primaries wrapped up last week, cementing Sununu and Pappas as their parties’ respective nominees. Pappas was the moderate choice in the Democratic primary, besting progressive candidate Karishma Manzur. 

Sununu, who served one term in the Senate, is the brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu (R), and their father, also named John, was the state’s governor in the 1980s and chair of the state Republican party.

data.title: House Democrats demand answers from CDC on Pennsylvania measles deaths
data.description:
House Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee are demanding answers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention regarding the agency’s refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s reporting of two measles deaths, the first in 35 years. 

The committee’s ranking member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) sent a letter to new agency director Erica Schwartz, calling for a briefing on CDC’s measles response, including why it hasn’t counted Pennsylvania’s deaths in its official weekly tally. 

Pallone was joined on the letter by Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo), ranking member of the health subcommittee, and Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), ranking member of the oversight and investigations subcommittee. 

They are demanding a staff briefing from CDC by Sept. 28. 

The decision to exclude the deaths reportedly came directly from Schwartz, who took charge of the agency this month amid a pledge to operate independently from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 

As of Friday, the CDC reported 160 new measles cases in the past week, bringing this year’s total to 3,294. But according to CDC, there have been no deaths.   

On its website, the agency put an asterisk next to the data and noted that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) hasn’t recorded any deaths this year where measles was the underlying cause.  

The Pennsylvania health department on Tuesday said it has now confirmed two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the state’s total to four. 

“Your decision to interfere with the inclusion of the first two measles related deaths on CDC’s publicly facing database is consistent with the many other ways that the Trump Administration has degraded tools to prevent disease spread, damaged the partnership between the states and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and suppressed information about threats and harm to the public,” the Democrats wrote. 

The third death “underscores the gravity of CDC’s failure to provide consistent, reliable information to the public as the country grapples with a historic return of measles,” the lawmkers wrote.  

Schwartz has not publicly discussed her reasoning for excluding a state’s own reporting, a radical departure from the agency’s normal practice. 

The state’s health department said it provided CDC with the relevant epidemiological data and evaluated the deaths based on CDC’s criteria.

data.title: 'Real Housewives of Salt Lake City' star says show to feature her Capitol Hill advocacy work
data.description:
Capitol Hill could soon be playing a supporting role on “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” after one of its stars, Angie Katsanevas, says she filmed some of her advocacy work in the nation’s capital for the show. 

“We did film some [of the time] that I spent here in D.C. working with the International Franchise Association (IFA),” Katsanevas, known to viewers as Angie K., told ITK this week.

“So yes, we’ll definitely see some of that” on the series’ seventh season, premiering this week on Bravo, she added.

ITK caught up with Katsanevas on Tuesday as she spoke at the IFA’s advocacy summit in Washington to honor its franchisees of the year award recipients. 

The visit marked Katsanevas’s second trip from the Beehive State to the Capitol this year. She advocated for the American Franchise Act — which proponents say would “strengthen the franchise model by providing clear, consistent standards for franchisors under federal labor law” — and testified at a House Small Business Committee hearing focused on franchising in January.

She said that she planned on making a return visit to the Capitol on Tuesday to meet with lawmakers. The conversations might also include “some hair tips and a few spoilers” from this “Real Housewives” season, she quipped. 

Katsanevas, who hosts the “GoDaddy School of Hustle” podcast, said grit is the name of the game in D.C.

“Everyone’s hustling here. They’re hustling to make a difference. They’re hustling to work towards putting this spotlight on the American Franchise Act. They’re hustling to push this bill to the finish line,” Katsanevas said.

When asked her expert assessment of the hair situation among lawmakers at the Capitol, the salon pro suggested that Congress has got their locks on lock.

“Looking fabulous,” Katsanevas, 52, exclaimed.

“Actually, I’m pretty surprised,” she added.

“Growing up, I would have not pictured that there were so many stylish women up here looking fabulous in their dresses and suits with great hair. So, I’m impressed,” Katsanevas said.

“D.C. is pretty progressive,” she said.

data.title: Trump disses 'hostile and conflicted' judge who blocked Kennedy Center renaming
data.description:
President Trump on Tuesday slammed the federal judge who blocked his administration’s latest effort to add his name to the Kennedy Center. 

The president, who has repeatedly criticized judges who rule against his administration, called U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper a “very hostile and conflicted Judge” shortly after the Obama appointee released his opinion in this case. 

“Isn’t that too bad? We have already wasted more than 6 months ‘playing around’ in Court,” the president wrote on Truth Social. “Time is our Enemy! The Board, comprised of some of the most prominent and respected people in our Nation, is meeting again today. It will be interesting to see what happens.”

The president said the iconic performing arts center is “in a virtual state of collapse,” citing the recent damage to the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer ceiling after a heavy rain storm in the nation’s capital. 

Cooper ruled Tuesday that the performing arts center’s board could not move forward with these renaming plans until it gets “Congress’s blessing” and found that the board’s August vote approving the addition of Trump’s name likely violated his earlier injunction. 

The federal judge ruled in May that the president’s name must be removed from the building’s facade. Trump’s Justice Department made several unsuccessful attempts to pause this order, and the lettering was ultimately removed in June. 

The Trump administration has exerted pressure to make a series of changes to the Kennedy Center. Last year, the president removed half of the center’s traditionally-bipartisan board, replaced these members with allies to his administration and named himself as the new chair. 

These changes have been opposed by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who challenged the Trump administration in a lawsuit. 

“The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial,” Beatty said in a statement following Cooper’s ruling. 

“The Court just rejected this proposal for the second time,” she continued. “This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop.”

data.title: Blanche dodges question on whether he asked for DiGenova's resignation
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dodged a question Tuesday about whether he asked for the resignation of Trump-ally Joe diGenova from the Justice Department amid reports that there was a tense phone call between the two before the lawyer’s departure.

“I don’t want to talk about communications I have with prosecutors. It’s not fair to them. It’s not fair to the process,” Blanche told reporters as he led a White House press briefing in the Rose Garden.

“He resigned last week. He came out of retirement to help the president, and to help us and we are very appreciative of the work that he did,” he continued.

DiGenova was tapped in April to lead an investigation into several of President Trump’s perceived enemies. He resigned last week, suggesting he was being asked to move too fast on the cases.

Asked why he resigned, diGenova told The Associated Press: “There’s plenty of evidence in all of these cases to prove the theories of prosecution. It just takes time to get there, and some people want to get there a little faster than others — and you can’t do that.”

In another interview with the New York Post, he said: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”

CNN reported Monday that diGenova resigned a day after a tense phone conversation with Blanche, citing sources familiar.

Blanche noted that diGenova said “some different things to different outlets, which is fine.”

“I very much appreciate the work that he did for us and for the administration,” he said. “Any investigations that he’s working of course continue, like they do, like any investigation does when somebody leaves. And we’re not going to slow down just because somebody leaves.”

Prosecutors on the case have reportedly focused on former CIA Director John Brennan and have also pursued information about those who worked on the Mar-a-Lago classified documents case against the president during the Biden administration.

data.title: Blanche dismisses concerns about Trump Jr's wedding gift from Putin ally
data.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns over a wedding gift to Donald Trump Jr. from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this year. 

“The president’s son has said that he’s a very close friend, and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding,” Blanche told reporters at the White House press briefing when asked if it was appropriate for Trump Jr. to accept the gift and if he would investigate if everything was appropriately reported as a gift. 

“When you say ‘am I investigating?’ Am I investigating what? And when you say this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know if that’s true or not,” he continued. “I like that it’s fun to talk about this issue and the rhetoric around it, but I think all of the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it.” 

“I don’t have any information. I don’t know this person either,” he said. 

ProPublica reported on Monday that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded Trump Jr. and wife Bettina Anderson’s lavish wedding festivities in the Bahamas, which included a private island and a fireworks show. 

Democrats and critics were quick to lash out at the Trump administration over potential ethics violations and national security concerns. 

Anderson, who is now Bettina Trump, responded to the fallout over the report in an Instagram post defending the wedding. 

“Our friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” the post read. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”

The president did not attend the wedding, but said in a statement to the New York Times that he had “no idea” who Kremlev was and said that the Russian oligarch “didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”

data.title: How IRS's 2027 tax brackets may change, according to new projections
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) — Inflation may remain top of mind for you, with the latest report showing rates holding steady through August. As pesky as it may be, it may also lead to yet another adjustment in our tax brackets, according to a new prediction.

The IRS typically announces changes that will impact how you file taxes each fall. Potentially the most impactful to most taxpayers is the adjustment to tax brackets.

That announcement came in early October last year, when the IRS released the federal brackets for 2026, which apply to the returns we will file next year.

In a few weeks, the IRS is expected to share what the tax brackets will be for the 2027 filing season. These adjustments are meant to address “bracket creep,” which occurs when your income goes up faster than the tax thresholds built into the IRS code, potentially causing your tax bill to increase. Without a threshold adjustment, inflation could offset wage gain and taxpayers could find themselves paying higher taxes without real income growth.

A report from Bloomberg Tax suggests the IRS could enact a 3.2% increase for 2027 due to inflation, up from the 2.7% increase rolled out last year.

Bloomberg’s report estimates that all seven tiers of the IRS’s tax brackets will see a bump in 2027:

It’s worth noting, though, that these are only projections (Bloomberg Tax’s projections for 2026, however, were in line with the true brackets). The actual updates to tax provisions aren’t expected from the IRS for at least a few more weeks.

If the tax brackets do change as expected, you’ll likely also see a larger paycheck in 2027.

The tax filing deadline in 2027 is April 15.
